accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE KS3 science programme of study (current, potential difference, resistance as the ratio of p.d. to current) and AQA GCSE Physics 8463 section 4.2.1.3 (V = IR, ohmic conductors, filament lamp I–V curve). Every number was recomputed: 6 V across 2/3/6/12 Ω gives 3/2/1/0.5 A; a 4 Ω resistor at 2/4/6/8 V gives 0.5/1/1.5/2 A; 0.1 Ω per cm on 3 V gives 0.5 A at 60 cm and 1.5 A at 20 cm; the 20 Ω and 5 Ω lines reach 0.5 A and 2 A at 10 V; the challenge answers are 0.5 A and 20 Ω. Parameterised items (i×r, 2n÷2, 5n×0.2, 3n÷3) are exact at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips IOP's Supporting Physics Teaching (electric circuits) and AQA examiner reports flag for V = IR: thinking more resistance gives more current (swap step prediction, sorter cards, challenge tag same), dividing the wrong way R ÷ V (triangle tag flip, challenge flip/flipR, mastery m6), multiplying when V is given (tags mul/times), adding amps to ohms (tag add), reading a steeper I–V line as more resistance (slope prediction, tag steep, practice p5) and mixing units (tags unitI/unitV, mastery m3).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagohm is built for this topic: a live circuit with an ammeter and moving charge dots where resistor cards swap in, an I–V plotter that only draws the line once four readings are in, a cover-the-letter V = IR triangle with three calculations, a resistance wire with a draggable crocodile clip and current targets, and a tap-the-line slope reader that includes a curving filament lamp. It shares no mechanics with flagcirc (meter placement) or flagseries (series vs parallel); the gate reports under 30% shingle overlap.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is found before it is named. Trying all four resistors shows the current halving as resistance doubles, then the caption states I = 6 V ÷ R. Plotting four points shows the straight line through the origin before proportionality is named. The wire step makes the learner find 60 cm and 20 cm by sliding the clip, so length and resistance become linked by their own result. The slope step has them pick lines by resistance, which builds the steep-means-low reading.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions come before the evidence: what happens to the current when resistance doubles (halves), what happens when voltage doubles on one resistor (doubles), what a longer wire does to resistance (goes up), and what a steeper I–V line means (less resistance). Each is revealed by the learner's own readings, and the reveal quotes their locked choice back with 'spot on' or a correction that explains the physics.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Every wrong option in the challenge has its own message naming the slip and showing the right working: for example 'That is R ÷ V. Current is V ÷ R: 9 ÷ 18 = 0.5 A' for flip, and messages for times, flipR, unitI, unitV, length, same and steep. The triangle step's wrong answers (div, add, mul, flip, sub) each give the correct rearrangement with numbers, and the wire step says whether the current is too big or too small for the clip position.

readability.evidence: The learner kid paragraphs score Flesch–Kincaid 2.5 (target ≤6.5) and the adult notes 8.9 (≤9.5), both measured by the pipeline. Canvas captions are one short instruction, symbols are always paired with words (Ω with ohms, A with amps), and the screen-reader summary spells out units in full. Numbers are kept to whole values or simple halves, so the reading load stays on the idea.

no_filler.evidence: Every step adds a new piece of the topic: the resistance–current link, proportionality, rearranging V = IR, wire length, I–V slopes with a non-ohmic lamp, then a mixed challenge. There are no mascots, decorative animations or repeated drills; the moving charge dots carry meaning because their speed tracks the current, and they are turned off under reduced motion.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 in light and dark themes with the pipeline browser walk and screenshots: the resistor and voltage cards are at least 32 px tall, the clip is a large drag handle that also has ±10 cm buttons, the slope lines can be tapped or chosen by buttons, and the I–V voltage cards hide once all four readings are in so the feedback box never covers them. The canvas keeps a light card in dark mode for contrast.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a matching DOM button with an aria-label (resistor cards, voltages, triangle covers, wire nudges, line choices, challenge answers), A.gest handles pointer drag, and each change is announced through the live region and the canvas aria-label with units spelled out. The axe checks pass in both themes on desktop and phone, colour is never the only cue (lines are labelled and the lamp is dashed), and reduced motion stops the charge dots.
